st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source reports record employment for 2024 law graduates and a prospective concern about absorbing larger cohorts, which is consistent with the cluster’s caution against claims of current profession-wide displacement. However, it does not examine AI exposure, causation, task reallocation, verification or operating-model redesign, so its position on the cluster’s principal proposition cannot be determined.

st.t: Graduate hiring: Strong outcomes mask entry contraction
st.an: The source directly supports the synthesis: it reports record Class of 2024 employment while distinguishing employment rates from market capacity and warning that smaller summer classes, weaker federal hiring and cohort size could produce fewer entry-level opportunities. Its contraction claims are forecasts rather than evidence of AI-caused displacement.

kp.k: Record graduate employment despite a substantially larger class
kp.d: Danielle A. Taylor reports employment outcomes approximately ten months after graduation, as of March 17, 2025. Among 37,815 graduates with known employment status, 93.4% were employed, up 0.8 percentage points from 2023. Graduating class size increased 10.6%, while jobs obtained increased 10.9%. These are legal graduate labour-market findings; the document does not attribute them to AI.

kp.k: Attorney employment and full-time outcomes reached new highs
kp.d: Bar admission required/anticipated employment reached 84.3% of graduates, rising 2.2 percentage points and setting a record under classifications introduced in 2001. Full-time, long-term employment in this category reached 83.4%, up 2.3 percentage points from 2023 and approximately 26 points from 57% in 2011. Taylor identifies growth in public defender, prosecutor and large-firm associate positions as drivers of increased attorney employment. Overall, 98.0% of jobs were full-time; unemployment, including those seeking and not seeking work, fell to 5.1%.

kp.k: Record employment rates conceal a smaller historical market
kp.d: Nikia L. Gray cautions that employment percentages depend on class size. Although the 2024 cohort secured record employment rates, it obtained nearly 1,800 fewer jobs than the 2007 cohort, leaving the entry-level market nearly 5% smaller than before the Great Recession. With applications at their highest level in nearly 15 years and another large class expected in 2027, Gray recommends caution before enrolling an equally large Class of 2028. This is a capacity warning, not a finding of AI displacement.

kp.k: Private practice exceeded its pre-recession employment peak
kp.d: Private practice employed 20,810 graduates, exceeding the 2007 record of 20,611 and adding more than 2,260 jobs over 2023. Its 58.9% share of employed graduates was the highest since 1992. Firms with more than 500 lawyers employed a record 7,126 graduates, nearly 760 more than in 2023, but their private-practice job share edged down from 34.3% to 34.2%, the first non-increase since 2011.

kp.k: Smaller firms contributed substantial growth without proven structural change
kp.d: Gray reports nearly 1,150 additional jobs at firms of 100 or fewer lawyers, compared with about 750 at firms above 500 lawyers, and suggests the smaller-firm growth may be opportunistic rather than sustained. Taylor reports that firms of 10 or fewer lawyers, including solo practitioners, accounted for 26.4% of law-firm jobs versus 28.0% in 2023; firms of 11–250 lawyers increased their share from 30.9% to 32.4%. Firms above 500 lawyers exceeded firms of 1–10 lawyers by nearly 1,800 jobs, whereas during 2011–2013 the smallest firms employed more than twice as many graduates as the largest.

kp.k: Salary records coexist with bimodality and reporting bias
kp.d: Salary information covered 72.6% of reported full-time jobs lasting at least one year. The national median reached $95,000, up 5.6%, and the mean reached $125,926, up 3.1%. The salary graph uses 24,937 reported salaries: 53.0% fell between $55,000 and $100,000, while 18.7% were at $225,000 and 4.4% at $215,000. NALP cautions that more complete large-firm salary reporting overstates the unadjusted mean by an estimated 5.7%; its adjusted mean is $119,112. Neither mean represents a common salary outcome.

kp.k: Private-practice median decline reflects composition, not widespread cuts
kp.d: The private-practice median fell 3.0% to $160,000, its first decline since 2011, after increasing 25.5% between 2021 and 2023. Taylor attributes the decline to changes in firm-size distribution, mergers and acquisitions affecting firm categorisation, and improved small- and mid-sized-firm salary reporting rather than widespread starting-salary cuts. Medians rose in most firm-size categories: firms above 500 lawyers reached $225,000, up 4.7%, while firms of 1–10 lawyers reached $80,000, up 6.7%. Firms of 51–100 lawyers were unchanged; firms of 251–500 lawyers declined 2.6%.

kp.k: Non-firm salaries increased across employment sectors
kp.d: Median salaries rose in every sector outside private practice. Government recorded the largest percentage increase, 8.7%, reaching $79,900. Public interest reached $72,000, up 8.1%; business reached $100,000, up 5.3%; judicial clerkships reached $70,000, up 4.5%; and education reached $64,000, up 4.9%.

kp.k: Business and JD Advantage employment shares declined
kp.d: JD Advantage positions accounted for 6.9% of graduates, down 0.9 percentage points and the lowest share since 2003. Business accounted for 7.0% of jobs, its lowest share since 1990 and the fifth-largest employer category. Within business, 32.6% of jobs required or anticipated bar admission and 47.0% were JD Advantage positions. Investment banking/financial institutions represented 12.8% of business jobs; in-house lawyers were the most commonly reported business job type, at 22.6%. Taylor interprets declining non-attorney employment partly in terms of graduates preferring attorney positions when available.

kp.k: Public service expanded, especially government and public interest
kp.d: Public service, including government and military jobs, judicial clerkships and public interest, accounted for 32.7% of jobs, exceeded historically only by 34.0% in 1975. Government added 739 jobs, public interest added 326 and judicial clerkships added 223. Public interest reached a record 3,421 jobs. Larger graduate numbers mean these gains did not uniformly increase employment shares: government rose to 12.9%, public interest remained at 9.7%, and clerkships fell 0.4 percentage points to 10.0%.

kp.k: Low job-search rates suggest, rather than measure, satisfaction
kp.d: Only 6.8% of employed graduates were seeking another job, a record low compared with 24.6% in 2011. NALP interprets this as an indication of satisfaction, not as a direct satisfaction-survey result. Job-search rates differed sharply: 30.0% of graduates in JD Advantage positions sought another job, compared with 4.2% in bar admission required/anticipated positions. Separately, 65.0% of employed graduates worked in the state where they attended law school; the Mid-Atlantic region accounted for 21.9% of jobs.

kp.k: School-funded jobs remained a small employment component
kp.d: School-funded jobs increased from 400 in 2023 to 453 in 2024, remaining 1.3% of all jobs and far below 2011 and 2013 levels. Of 2024 funded jobs, 67.3% required bar licensure, 9.7% were part-time and 12.8% lasted less than one year; 63.1% were full-time, long-term and required bar licensure, versus fewer than 8% in 2011. Public interest and education accounted for 79.2% of funded jobs. Education employment rose from 457 to 484 jobs but remained about one-third of its 2009–2010 peak; school funding supported 27.7% of 2024 education jobs.

kp.k: Hiring contraction is forecast, not established for subsequent cohorts
kp.d: Taylor predicts reduced BigLaw hiring for the Classes of 2025 and 2026, citing separate NALP recruiting research showing smaller 2024 and 2025 summer associate intake. Federal hiring freezes and rescinded Honors-program offers are expected to reduce 2025 federal employment, a sector typically accounting for about 3% of graduate jobs. Federal spending cuts could also constrain state, local and public-interest hiring. Gray similarly anticipates reversal of government and public-interest gains. Taylor qualifies this outlook: the 2025 and 2026 cohorts entered with nearly 5,000 fewer 1Ls than the 2024 cohort, potentially preserving relatively resilient employment outcomes despite fewer jobs.
